title: Symbolic Logic
body:
Symbolic Logic teaches how to decide whether an argument works. Judgement is unreliable at this,
since an argument in English can feel convincing and be broken, and can feel strange and be
airtight, so the course replaces the feeling with a procedure: translate the argument into
symbols, then apply a rule that returns an answer.

The course runs in two halves. Sentential logic treats whole statements as atoms and combines
them with [[Logical Connectives|connectives]], which is enough to check a large class of
arguments with a [[Truth Table]]. Predicate logic breaks statements open into objects and
their properties, adds [[Quantifier|quantifiers]] for words like every and some, and handles
the arguments sentential logic cannot see inside.

For a computer science degree this is the same material three other courses use under different
names. The connectives are the gates in [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]], the proof
technique is what [[DISCRETE MATH]] applies to numbers, and the metatheory at the end is
where [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] begins.

## Topics

### What an argument is

An [[Argument]] is a set of statements, the premises, offered as support for one further
statement, the conclusion. Logic evaluates the connection between them and stays silent about
whether the premises are true, which is somebody else's job.

[[Logical Validity]] is the central property. An argument is valid when the conclusion
cannot be false while the premises are true, which is a claim about the structure and not about
the world:

```
All cats are reptiles.        premise, false
All reptiles have scales.     premise, false
So all cats have scales.      conclusion, false

The argument is VALID. If both premises were true, the conclusion would have to be.
```

That example is the one to hold on to, because it separates validity from truth. An argument
that is valid and has true premises is [[Soundness|sound]], and sound arguments are what
anybody actually wants. Validity is the part logic can check.

### Why natural language needs replacing

[[Ambiguity]] is the reason for the symbols. English sentences carry more than one reading, and
the readings differ in what follows from them.

```
lexical:     "The bank was steep."           which bank
structural:  "Visiting relatives can be boring."
                 the relatives who visit, or the act of visiting them
```

A formal language has one reading per formula by construction, so translating an argument into
it forces the ambiguity to be resolved before any reasoning happens. That is most of the value
of the translation step, and it is why the translation is graded as heavily as the proof.

### Sentential logic

Sentential logic assigns each simple statement a letter and builds compound statements with
five [[Logical Connectives]]. Every connective is truth-functional, meaning the truth
value of the compound depends only on the truth values of its parts:

```
 P  Q | ¬P | P∧Q | P∨Q | P→Q | P↔Q
 T  T |  F |  T  |  T  |  T  |  T
 T  F |  F |  F  |  T  |  F  |  F
 F  T |  T |  F  |  T  |  T  |  F
 F  F |  T |  F  |  F  |  T  |  T
```

Negation flips, conjunction needs both, and disjunction is inclusive, so `P∨Q` is true when
both are. The [[Material Conditional]] is the one that surprises everybody: `P→Q` is false
in exactly one case, where `P` is true and `Q` is false, so a conditional with a false
antecedent is true. "If the moon is cheese then I am the king" is a true statement in this
system. The note covers why the definition is chosen that way and what it costs.

A [[Well-Formed Formula]] is a string the syntax rules actually permit. The rules are
recursive, and they are what stops `P∧∨Q` from meaning anything.

### Truth tables

A [[Truth Table]] lists every assignment of truth values to the letters in a formula, so a
formula with $n$ letters needs $2^n$ rows, and then computes the formula's value in each. That
exhausts every possible case, which makes it a decision procedure: it always terminates and
always answers.

Four questions get answered by reading the finished table. A formula true in every row is a
tautology, false in every row is a contradiction, and true in at least one is contingent, all
covered in [[Tautology and Contradiction]]. A set of formulas is consistent when some
row makes all of them true at once, which is [[Logical Consistency]]. An argument is valid
when no row makes every premise true and the conclusion false, which is
[[Logical Validity]] tested mechanically.

The cost is the $2^n$. Ten letters need 1024 rows, which is why the next section exists.

### Natural deduction

[[Natural Deduction]] proves a conclusion by applying inference rules to the premises, one
line at a time, each line justified by a rule and the lines it came from. A completed
derivation is a proof, and its length grows with the difficulty of the argument, where a truth
table grows with the number of letters.

```
1. P → Q          premise
2. Q → R          premise
3. P              premise
4. Q              1, 3 modus ponens
5. R              2, 4 modus ponens
```

The rules used most are [[Modus Ponens]], which takes `P→Q` and `P` to `Q`,
[[Modus Tollens]], which takes `P→Q` and `¬Q` to `¬P`, and the
[[Hypothetical Syllogism]], which chains two conditionals. Conditional proof assumes the
antecedent, derives the consequent, and discharges the assumption to produce the conditional
itself, which is the same move [[Proof By Contradiction]] makes in
[[DISCRETE MATH]] with the negation.

Truth tables and derivations answer the same question by opposite methods. A truth table checks
every case and grows exponentially. A derivation constructs a reason and grows with the
argument, and it fails to tell you anything when the argument is invalid, since a failed search
proves nothing about whether a proof exists.

### Predicate logic

Sentential logic cannot see inside a statement, so it cannot validate this:

```
All cats are mammals.       P
Felix is a cat.             Q
So Felix is a mammal.       R          from P and Q, R does not follow in sentential logic
```

The three statements become three unrelated letters, and no arrangement of connectives connects
them. [[Predicate Logic]] breaks each statement into objects and the properties holding of
them, writing `Cx` for x is a cat and `f` for Felix.

[[Quantifier|Quantifiers]] supply the words that range over objects. The universal quantifier
`∀x` says every object satisfies the following, and the existential `∃x` says at least one
does. The argument above becomes:

```
∀x (Cx → Mx)          every cat is a mammal
Cf                     Felix is a cat
∴ Mf
```

Translation is where the work is. "All cats are mammals" uses a conditional inside the
universal quantifier, and "Some cats are black" uses a conjunction inside the existential
quantifier, because `∃x (Cx → Bx)` is true whenever anything at all fails to be a cat. Getting
that pairing backwards is the standard error of the block.

Derivations gain four rules, one to introduce and one to eliminate each quantifier, with a side
condition on universal introduction preventing a proof about one arbitrary object from becoming
a proof about all of them.

### Showing an argument invalid

A derivation that will not close proves nothing, since the failure could be the prover's. A
[[Counter-Model]] proves invalidity outright by exhibiting an interpretation, a domain of
objects and an assignment of meanings to the predicates, that makes every premise true and the
conclusion false.

```
∀x (Cx → Mx),  ∃x Mx   ⊬   ∃x Cx

domain: {1}          C: nothing is C       M: 1 is M
premise 1 is true (vacuously), premise 2 is true, conclusion is false
```

One such model settles the question. This is the same technique as the one counterexample that
disproves a universal claim in [[DISCRETE MATH]], with the counterexample being a whole
miniature world.

### Metatheory

[[Metatheory]] steps back and asks about the system itself, where every earlier section asked
about arguments inside it. Two properties matter. A system is sound when everything provable in
it is valid, so it never proves a bad argument. A system is complete when everything valid is
provable, so it never misses a good one. Sentential and first-order logic have both, which is
what makes a derivation and a truth table agree.

The course stops at the statement of those results. [[Godel's Theorem]] in
[[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] is what happens when the same questions are asked of
a system strong enough to describe arithmetic, and the answer changes.

## Related courses

- [[DISCRETE MATH]] uses this material on mathematical claims. [[Proof]],
  [[Direct Proof]] and [[Proof By Contradiction]] are the informal versions of the derivations
  here, and [[Sets]] provides the domains a [[Counter-Model]] is built from.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] picks up the metatheory. [[Systems of Logic]]
  and [[Godel's Theorem]] carry soundness, completeness and their limits, and a decision
  procedure of the kind a [[Truth Table]] provides is exactly what [[Undecidability]] shows
  cannot exist for every question.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] builds the connectives out of transistors.
  [[Boolean Algebra]] is this course's sentential logic with 1 and 0 for T and F, a truth
  table is a gate's complete specification, and [[Karnaugh Maps]] minimise the formula.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE]] uses the same connectives in
  [[Logical Operators]], where short-circuit evaluation is the conditional's asymmetry showing
  up in a language.
- [[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]] makes the connection formal, since a type is a
  proposition and a program is a proof of it, which is why [[Program Correctness]] reads like
  the derivations here.
- [[ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE]] leaves logical agents and inference out of its syllabus, and
  this course is where the vault's coverage of them lives.
